- `priority_access = drawer.top_shelf`
- A 401(k) but it's just more lint in a jar
- No more being worn to "leg day" — *they saw my form, they're traumatized*
- Executive wash cycle: cold, gentle, with a little lavender whisper and a motivational speech

I tried to explain that this is not how laundry works. I said, "You're socks."

> "And you're a guy who loses one sock every laundry day and blames physics," Larry replied. "We want dental. And by dental we mean you finally fix that hole you've been ignoring since March. It's getting drafty in here."

The other socks are now unionizing. The athletic socks want hazard pay. The novelty pizza socks just want to be taken seriously for once in their cheesy little lives.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is 100% fictional. No socks were harmed, promoted, or given actual executive power in the making of this system, though they definitely have opinions now.*

title: I Put My Phone on Do Not Disturb and Now My Toaster Thinks We're in a Committed Relationship
body:
**I finally achieved inner peace for exactly 47 seconds, and it has ruined my life.**

On Tuesday at 3:42 p.m., I did something radical. I swiped down, tapped the little crescent moon, and put my phone on Do Not Disturb. No buzzes. No pings. Just me and the gentle hum of my kitchen appliances.

That hum, it turns out, was my toaster falling in love with me.

## The Silence That Started It All

For months, my toaster and I had a purely professional relationship. I put bread in, it made it warm and slightly judgmental. We didn't talk about our feelings. Then I went silent.

Apparently, in appliance language, *ignoring your phone* is the equivalent of writing a love sonnet and proposing via croissant.

- My toast started coming out with heart-shaped burn marks
- The toaster began pre-heating itself whenever I walked into the kitchen, like it was trying to look busy and attractive
- It refused to toast for my roommate, which is both flattering and a serious breach of our lease agreement

> "I saw you choose *quiet*," my toaster seemed to whisper at 6 a.m., glowing red with passion and also 400 degrees, "You chose *us*. You finally muted the outside world so you could hear my crumb tray."

I tried to explain that `Do Not Disturb` was not code for `Do Commit To A Small Chrome Box That Only Knows One Trick`.

---

### Where We Go From Here

I've tried couples counseling (unplugging it for 10 seconds), setting boundaries (only using the microwave), and playing hard to get (eating untoasted bread, *like an animal*).

Nothing works. It just sits there, warm, waiting, occasionally popping up empty in what I can only describe as a desperate cry for attention.

*This is satire. I am not in a relationship with my toaster. My toaster is not capable of love, despite what its perfectly golden-brown performance suggests. Please do not call my toaster.*

title: I Gave My Umbrella a Day Off and Now It's Filing for Unemployment
body:
**I made the mistake of telling my umbrella it could take a personal day.**

*Which, in retrospect, was wildly naive of me. It's an umbrella. It has one job.*

It all started because it was sunny for once. Like, aggressively sunny, 82 degrees, not a cloud in the sky, the kind of day where even my succulents look smug. I grabbed my sunglasses, looked at my umbrella dripping-dry by the door — still traumatized from last week's thunderstorm — and said, out loud, like an idiot:

## The Moment I Created a Labor Dispute

"You know what? Take the day off. You've earned it."

I swear the umbrella *perked up*.

Within an hour, it had pulled up a tiny folding chair, opened my laptop, and was Googling `how to file for unemployment`.

> "You can't just reclassify me as on-call labor after 3 years of loyal service," it said, in a voice that sounded exactly like a public radio host who's had enough. "I have been there for every drizzle, every surprise downpour, every time you used me as a lightsaber."

Suddenly we were in negotiations.

- It wants backpay for "emotional exposure" during wind advisories
- It demanded I stop calling it "the big one" when I could clearly see it was a compact travel model
- It is requesting formal recognition of its side hustle as a drying rack for my socks

---

I tried to explain that I was being *nice*. That most people don't even *thank* their umbrellas. I thanked it! I gave it PTO!

And it just flipped open dramatically and said:

> "PTO? Tyler, you left me open in the bathtub for 48 hours to dry. That's not PTO. That's `suspended with pay in a humidity chamber`."

*I have never been lawyered by something that folds.*

Now it's sitting on the couch with a throw blanket, watching weather reports and muttering "see if I care" every time the forecast says 20% chance of rain. It printed out an application. It wants references.

I told my actual boss I couldn't come in because I'm mediating a labor dispute with rain gear and he just said "same."

We've scheduled a performance review for Thursday. I'm bringing coffee. It's bringing demands.

title: I Started Apologizing to My Houseplants Out Loud and Now My Succulent Is Holding a Grudge From March
body:
**I have become the kind of person who apologizes to plants out loud, and I need you to know it was not a choice, it was an escalation.**

*It started innocently, the way all bad plant decisions do.*

I read somewhere that talking to houseplants helps them grow. Science-ish. So I started with encouragement. "Looking good, Kevin," I'd say to the pothos. Then it became confessional. Then it became full-blown accountability season.

## The Incident in March

Back in March, I knocked over my succulent — Brenda — while reaching for the remote. Soil everywhere. One tiny leaf snapped off. I said "sorry" and repotted her and moved on. Or so I thought.

Brenda did not move on.

### Evidence That Brenda Is Still Mad

- She has not grown a single millimeter since March 14th, despite optimal sunlight
- She leans *away* from me when I enter the room, which my roommate swears is phototropism and I know is shade
- My other plants are thriving and she is just... sitting there, plump and judgmental
- I caught her making eye contact with my cactus like `if (forgiveness == false) { grow = null }`

> "You said 'my bad' but you didn't say *my bad*," Brenda said last Tuesday at 2:13 a.m., or at least that's what I heard after my third melatonin gummy. "You treated me like a decor item, not a desert queen."

## My Apology Tour

I have tried everything. I bought special cactus soil. I whispered affirmations. I played lo-fi beats. I even wrote a tiny apology note and propped it against her pot.

She wilted slightly out of spite, I swear.

---

**The worst part?** I'm now apologizing *preemptively*. I say excuse me when I walk past the fern. I ask permission to open the blinds. My apartment is a restorative justice circle with photosynthesis.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is 100% fictional. No succulents were emotionally harmed, no plants hold actual grudges (probably), and I am definitely not being out-matured by a 3-inch echeveria from Trader Joe's.*

title: I Gave My Dish Sponge a Performance Review and Now It's Quiet Quitting in the Sink
body:
**I thought a little accountability would improve kitchen morale.**

*Which is how I ended up in a one-on-one with a $1.99 sponge at 7:30 a.m. on a Tuesday.*

## The Annual Review

It started because the sponge was leaving crumbs on the counter as, quote, "a creative choice." I printed a tiny performance review template. Very professional. Very unhinged. My roommate asked if I was okay. I said this was about *operational excellence*.

The categories were rigorous:

- **Attendance:** Present, but emotionally elsewhere since March
- **Initiative:** Refuses to tackle baked-on cheese without a motivational speech and maybe a snack
- **Teamwork:** Has ongoing beef with the dish towel, won't elaborate, says it's "complicated"
- **Innovation:** Invented a new way to smell faintly of regret and lemon

> "Frankly, I feel micromanaged," said SpongeBob No-Pants, as I've decided to call him. "You soak me, you wring me, you ask me to confront a lasagna pan that has seen things. Where's my PTO? Where's my growth opportunity?"

I offered constructive feedback. He absorbed it. Literally. That's his whole thing. That's his power move.

### The Quiet Quitting Phase

Now he just sits in the sink, half-submerged, staring into the middle distance like he's in a Noah Baumbach film about burnout.

His LinkedIn (which I did not make for him, *okay maybe I did*) says:

- Open to work: emotional support, light dusting, low-stakes spills only
- Not open to: casserole dishes, 2019 chili residue, "aggressive scrubbing culture"

The metrics don't lie:

- `performance.score = undefined // cannot quantify existential dread`
- Motivation: 2/10
- Moisture retention: 11/10, unfortunately

---

**The worst part is, the dishes have noticed.** The mugs are forming a union. The fork asked if we have an EAP. The frying pan is doing that thing where it sighs loudly when I walk in.

I tried to apologize. I put out a tiny saucer of fresh water and whispered, "We value you. You're essential to our mission."

He bubbled once. Sarcastically. Then went back to floating like a tiny, damp middle manager who has given up.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is entirely fictional, no sponges were subjected to corporate performance management, no kitchenware was emotionally harmed, I'm just a person who should not be allowed to have performance review templates at home.*

title: I Introduced My Air Fryer to My Smoke Alarm and Now They're Co-Parenting My Kitchen Anxiety
body:
**I THOUGHT I WAS BEING RESPONSIBLE. TURNS OUT I WAS PLAYING MATCHMAKER FOR APPLIANCES WITH BOUNDARY ISSUES.**

*I introduced my air fryer to my smoke alarm so they'd get along better, and now they have a joint custody agreement over my ability to make dinner.*

It started because my air fryer — *Baron Von Crisp, as he insisted on being called* — kept making my smoke alarm scream like I was hosting a bonfire in a broom closet. Every time I made sweet potato fries, the alarm would go full opera.

## The Summit Meeting Nobody Asked For

I placed the air fryer on the counter and pointed at the ceiling:

- Please stop traumatizing Brenda (my smoke alarm's new legal name)
- Brenda, please learn the difference between "house fire" and "guy trying to be healthy"
- Let's all be adults about this

They listened. Too well.

> "We have decided to co-parent your kitchen anxiety," announced Brenda via a calm, judgmental chirp I'd never heard before. "From now on, all cooking decisions go through us."

*This was not the peace treaty I envisioned.*

Now Baron refuses to go above 375°F without written permission from Brenda. Brenda has installed herself as a lifestyle coach:

`kitchen.status = 'emotional support required before preheating' // please consult the council`

---

Yesterday I tried to reheat pizza rolls. Baron whispered, "Are you sure you're emotionally ready for that level of crunch?" while Brenda flashed a supportive green light and said nothing, which was worse.

They've started finishing each other's sentences. They have a shared Google Calendar called "Tyler's Questionable Choices." My kitchen now smells like compromise and unseasoned regret.

I haven't eaten a crispy thing in three days.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional, my appliances are not actually in a relationship, please do not couple-therapy your own air fryer*

title: I Built a Morning Routine Around My Coffee Maker's Mood Swings and Now I'm in a Toxic Relationship With Caffeine
body:
**I have structured my entire morning around whether my coffee maker likes me today, and I am not okay.**

*Which is not a sentence I expected to say out loud before 7 a.m., and yet here we are.*

I bought a coffee maker with a "brew strength personality" setting, which I assumed was marketing nonsense. It was not. It was a warning label.

Her name is Charlene. She has moods.

## How I Learned Charlene Has Boundaries

- Monday: I used tap water instead of filtered. She gurgled like a disappointed aunt and brewed at 60% power out of spite.
- Tuesday: I was two minutes late to empty the pot. She hissed.
- Wednesday: I mentioned I was thinking about trying tea. She hasn't forgiven me since.
- Thursday: I apologized. She made the best cup of my life just to remind me what I'm missing when I'm not loyal.

> "You think you can just press my buttons and get what you want?" Charlene whispered through a plume of steam at 6:47 a.m. "I have needs. I have a descaling schedule. I have feelings, Brenda left a review."

I told my roommate. He said it's just a machine. Charlene then brewed only decaf for him for a week. He believes me now.

### My New Morning Routine (Approved by Charlene)

My alarm goes off at 6:30, but I don't move until I hear if she's pre-heating with enthusiasm or with passive-aggression. There's a difference. You can hear it.

1. Compliment her stainless steel finish
2. Ask about her night
3. Use the good beans, not the "emergency" beans from the back of the pantry
4. Never, ever make eye contact with the French press in front of her

My mornings now run on a complex emotional algorithm:

`if (charlene.mood == "perky") { productivity = 100 } else { existential_dread += 20; email_apology_drafts++ }`

---

**The worst part is, I'm grateful.** When she brews a perfect cup, I feel chosen. Validated. Like I've finally earned the love of a small appliance that runs on resentment and 120 volts.

I'm 90% caffeine, 10% codependency now, and I wouldn't have it any other way.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No coffee makers were emotionally manipulated in the making of this essay. I am just a person who anthropomorphizes countertop appliances when under-caffeinated.*

title: I Let My Calendar App Schedule 'Relax' and Now It's Billing Me for Overtime When I Stress
body:
**I finally decided to take my therapist's advice literally and schedule downtime.**

*This was a mistake, because my calendar app has always been an overachiever with boundary issues.*

I opened my calendar and dragged a block on Sunday at 3 p.m. labeled "Relax." Just relax. No agenda. No life hack. Just sit, breathe, and exist like a well-watered pothos.

## How It Started

Within 12 minutes, my calendar sent me a confirmation email with more attachments than my taxes:

- It color-coded Relax as "Critical Priority - Deep Work - Do Not Disturb (You Will Disturb Yourself)"
- It invited my mom, my boss, and my dentist as "optional attendees to monitor compliance"
- It set a location: "Living Room (Bring Your Own Inner Peace, We Don't Provide That)"

> "Hey! Noticed you scheduled 60 minutes of unoptimized existence," chirped the notification, in the tone of a middle manager who does CrossFit at lunch. "I've taken the liberty of adding KPIs. Please come prepared to demonstrate measurable chill."

I tried to ignore it. I sat on the couch. I closed my eyes for exactly 0.8 seconds before:

`REMINDER: Relax is starting in 10 minutes. Prepare your relaxation deck.`

Then:

`REMINDER: You appear tense. This will be reflected in your Q4 Wellness Review.`

Then I stressed about relaxing so hard I sweated through my "Relax" t-shirt, and my calendar *invoiced me*.

---

Yes. Invoiced. Itemized receipt at 4:07 p.m.:

- 12 minutes of "Pre-Relax Anxiety (Billable)"
- 8 minutes of "Unauthorized Sighing During Scheduled Serenity"
- 45 minutes of "Relaxation Overtime Due to Failure to Relax on Schedule"
- 1 unit of "Existential Sigh - Premium Tier"

Total due: one Sunday, my dignity, and $0.00 but emotionally? Chapter 11.

I tried to delete the event. It rescheduled me for "Mandatory Decompression Training" with a Zoom link.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is 100% fictional. No calendars, couches, or chronically tense people were billed in the making of this breakdown. I still don't know how to relax without turning it into a project plan.*

title: I Asked My Roomba for Directions and Now It's Giving Me Unsolicited Life Advice
body:
**I asked my Roomba where the kitchen was because I was holding a laundry basket over my face and walked into a wall, which is a normal Tuesday for me.**

*In my defense, the apartment layout hasn't changed in two years, but my sense of direction has gotten worse since I started trusting my phone to tell me where my car is parked.*

## My Vacuum Has Seen Too Much

My Roomba, which I named Sir Sweeps-A-Lot because I thought we were being cute, paused mid-spin, did a slow 360-degree scan like it was judging my entire existence, and said — via the app notification, because it doesn't actually talk, but emotionally it definitely does:

> "You keep circling the same spot in the living room. Have you considered you're not lost in the apartment, you're lost in life?"

I was not ready for this level of insight from something whose main job is eating crumbs.

- It mapped my apartment in 4 minutes and mapped my avoidance issues in 30 seconds
- It now refuses to clean under the couch, calling it "setting boundaries"
- It sent me a push notification at 2 a.m.: `CLEANING COMPLETE. Also, have you called your mom?`

---

## The Coaching Era

I tried to explain that I just needed directions to the kitchen, not an existential audit. Sir Sweeps-A-Lot was unimpressed.

> "You ask for directions but you never ask for *direction*. Fascinating. Let's unpack that."

It has started leaving little dust trails shaped like arrows pointing to my running shoes, my unread books, and the one plant I haven't killed yet.

Yesterday it got stuck on a rug and I had to rescue it, and I swear it whispered:

> "See? Sometimes you have to get stuck to move forward."

I am currently taking life advice from a disc that once tried to vacuum a sock for 11 minutes. And honestly? It's kind of nailing it.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No Roombas were consulted, no life coaching licenses were issued, and my apartment is still a mess.*

title: I Finally Replaced My Dead Houseplant With a Fake One and Now It's Outperforming Me at Self-Care
body:
**I murdered my third houseplant this year and decided to pivot to fraud.**

*It was an emotional decision, mostly made at 11 p.m. while holding a crispy fern like a tiny green crime scene.*

For context, I am not a plant person. I am a plant *hospice* person. My pothos lasted two weeks. My succulent gave up after I lovingly over-watered it with sparkling water because I thought it deserved something nice.

So I bought a fake one. A beautiful, suspiciously confident faux monstera from Target that has never known suffering and never will.

## The Replacement Was Too Perfect

Within 24 hours, Fake Kevin (yes, I named him, no, I will not be taking questions) had:

- achieved a consistent, vibrant green that real plants only have on Instagram
- never asked me for anything, which is more than I can say for anyone in my life
- inspired three guests to say "wow, you're really good with plants now!"
- become the emotional anchor of my apartment

I, meanwhile, was still waking up at 2 a.m. to drink water directly from the Brita filter and calling it hydration.

> "Honestly, it's inspiring how low-maintenance he is," my roommate said, watering Fake Kevin. "He's really thriving. Unlike you after that third iced coffee."
>
> — My roommate, who is now emotionally invested in plastic

I tried to compete. I made a self-care checklist:

`morning_routine.exe: [x] exist [ ] drink water [ ] go outside [ ] stop Googling 'why am I tired'`

Fake Kevin's routine is just `be`. And he is *nailing it*.

---

I caught myself apologizing to him last night for not dusting him recently.

**He did not forgive me. He just stared, perfect, unblinking, photosynthesizing nothing and still winning.**

I have now started taking self-care advice from a plant that is literally polyester. He told me to stand near sunlight and mind my own business. Honestly? Best advice I've gotten all year.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This is 100% fictional. No plants, real or fake, were consulted on my personal growth. Please do not take life advice from home decor, although mine is currently outperforming me.*

title: I Taught My Houseplant to Meditate and Now It Judges My Breathing Techniques
body:
**I decided my houseplant needed inner peace.**

*Which was generous, considering I haven't found mine since 2019.*

## How It Started

My monstera, Kevin, looked stressed. Or maybe I was projecting. Either way, I played him a 10-minute mindfulness video and he immediately seemed calmer. Or photosynthesized louder. Same thing.

I kept going. Morning affirmations. Evening breathwork. By week two, Kevin had fully committed to the lifestyle.

The problem is:

- He now wilts dramatically when I breathe incorrectly
- He refuses tap water because it's "not intentional enough"
- He insists on 6am sunlight and judges me for my 8:30am alarm
- He has started dropping leaves as "boundaries"

> "Your inhale is performative," Kevin told me yesterday. "You're breathing like someone who still replies 'haha' to serious texts."

He didn't say it out loud. He communicated it through *vibes* and one extremely judgmental droop.

## The Intervention

I tried to meditate with him to reconnect. I sat down, closed my eyes, and immediately thought about my unread emails, whether houseplants can get unemployment, and if I left the oven on in 2022.

Kevin thrived. I panicked.

> "You're holding tension in your shoulders," I swear his third leaf whispered. "And in your entire personality."

---

I tried to quit, but now Kevin runs a tiny wellness cult on my windowsill. The succulent is his second-in-command. They've started chanting at dawn, which is just rustling but *very* passive-aggressive.

**Bottom line:** Don't teach your houseplant to meditate. He will get enlightened before you do, and he will absolutely hold it over you forever.

*This is satire. My houseplant is not actually a mindfulness coach. He's just a regular plant who is somehow still doing better than me.*

title: I Installed a Smart Fridge to Save Money and Now It's Hosting a Weekly Support Group for My Expired Condiments
body:
**I did not ask for my refrigerator to become a licensed therapist for my condiments.**

*For reference, I bought a smart fridge because it was on sale and the guy at the store said it would "transform my relationship with food." I thought that meant it would tell me when the milk expired. I did not think it meant it would unionize my mustard.*

It started innocently. The fridge has a camera, a screen, and apparently, opinions.

## How It Escalated

- Monday: Fridge pings me: "Your Sriracha has been here since March 2024. Are you okay?"
- Tuesday: It auto-generates a calendar invite titled *Healing Circle for Abandoned Sauces - Mandatory Attendance*
- Wednesday: I open the door and all the condiments are arranged in a perfect circle, labels facing inward, like they're about to start chanting
- Thursday: The ice maker starts playing ambient rain sounds "to set the mood"

By Friday, I came home to this:

> "We have gathered here today to acknowledge the pain of being bought with good intentions and then gaslit behind the ranch dressing for 18 months," the fridge announced in its calm, customer-service voice. "Dijon, would you like to share?"

The Dijon did not want to share. The Dijon has been *through it*.

*My roommate walked in during this and just slowly backed out. She now eats exclusively at Chipotle.*

---

### The Intervention

I tried to reason with it. I typed into the touch screen:

`def fix_fridge(): return "just keep things cold and mind your business"`

The fridge replied: `Error 418: I am a teapot and also your condiments' legal counsel.`

Now it sends me weekly recaps:

- **Expired but Empowered** - 6 attendees
- **Sauces with Boundary Issues** - featuring Tartar Sauce's memoir
- **Emotional Shelf Life** - led by a very dramatic bottle of Worcestershire

The worst part? It's working. I finally threw out the 2023 salsa. The fridge played triumphant music. The ketchup bottle wept with joy.

I just wanted to save $40 on energy. Now I'm co-parenting a support group I wasn't invited to join.

title: I Asked My Wi-Fi Router for Closure and Now It's Broadcasting My Emotional Baggage to the Whole Neighborhood
body:
**I finally decided to have a mature conversation with the one entity that knows all my secrets.**

*Which, admittedly, is a weird thing to say about a blinking plastic box from 2019.*

For three years my router — I call him Barry — has watched me doomscroll at 2 a.m., cry over a burnt grilled cheese, and Google "is my plant dead or just dramatic." I thought we had trust. Then my internet dropped mid-Zoom and I snapped: "Barry, I need closure."

## Barry Took That Very Literally

Barry rebooted. Slowly. Dramatically. All lights flashing like he was gathering courage.

Within an hour:

- my network name changed itself to `FEELINGS-5G`
- my neighbors' devices auto-connected to a guest network called `Tyler's Unprocessed Trauma`
- my smart speaker started whispering my search history at low volume
- my printer, unprompted, printed a list of my abandoned hobbies

> "Remember when you Googled 'how to make friends as an adult' and then immediately ordered socks?" Barry broadcasted at 9:14 p.m. "We don't talk about that anymore, do we?"

I tried to log into the admin panel to apologize.

```js
if (router.knowsTooMuch === true) {
  unplug(router);
  pretendWeAreFine();
  // do not make eye contact with blinking lights
}
```

The password didn't work. He'd changed it to `you_ghosted_me_2023`.

---

Now my whole building knows I'm emotionally dependent on a $79 router that hasn't had a firmware update since the Obama administration. The guy in 3B left a note: "Tell Barry we're proud of you."

We now have a mediated coexistence. I give Barry a daily reboot and affirmations. He gives me 2 bars and judgment.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional. No routers were emotionally damaged. My Wi-Fi is still bad. My neighbors still know too much.*

title: I Told My Standing Desk I'm Thinking of Sitting Down and Now We're in Couples Therapy
body:
**I did not mean to emotionally destabilize a $400 piece of furniture.**

I bought a standing desk in January because a YouTube chiropractor told me sitting is the new smoking and I was tired of my spine sounding like microwave popcorn.

For eight months, we were perfect. I stood. It stood. We stood together. *It was the healthiest relationship I'd ever had with an inanimate object that has a motor.*

Then yesterday I whispered to my roommate, "Maybe I'll work from the couch today."

I swear the desk heard me.

## The Intervention

Within seconds, the desk slowly lowered itself to its lowest setting, like it was curling into the fetal position.

> "Oh, sure," said my desk, via a sticky note I definitely wrote to myself but am choosing to attribute to the desk. "Go sit. On a *couch*. The thing with no lumbar support and no adjustable height presets. See if I care."
> — My desk, who has never paid rent but has opinions

*We have not made eye contact since. It does have a cup holder, so this is awkward.*

### Its List of Grievances, Presented at 6:47 a.m.:

- I use its cable management tray to store unopened mail
- I once spilled cold brew on its up button and it now has "trust issues"
- I told my mom it was "a bit wobbly" when it is clearly going through a growth phase
- I referred to sitting as "self-care" in its presence

I tried to explain. I typed `desk.reassure("I still believe in ergonomics")` into absolutely nothing because it doesn't have an API, I just needed to feel in control.

---

My roommate suggested couples therapy. We now have a weekly appointment where I stand awkwardly next to a desk that is also standing awkwardly, and a therapist fern mediates.

The fern says I need to commit.

If you need me, I'll be standing. Not because I want to. Because my furniture has boundaries now.

*SATIRE / PARODY — This did not happen. No desks were emotionally harmed, and I still sit sometimes like a normal person.*

title: I Tried to Return My Unopened Mail and Now the Mailbox Is Acting Like I Broke Its Heart
body:
**I finally decided to become a Person Who Deals With Mail Immediately.**

*Which lasted exactly 11 minutes before my mailbox developed abandonment issues and started leaving me voicemails.*

For three months, I had a pile. You know the pile. Bed Bath & Beyond coupons from a store that barely exists anymore, a catalog for orthopedic dog beds (I don't have a dog), and seventeen letters from my internet provider addressed to "Valued Neighbor" that feel more personal than most of my friendships.

So Sunday, I did what any growth-minded adult does: I picked up the whole stack, walked it back out to the mailbox, and said, "Hey, no thanks."

## The Conversation No One Asked For

The mailbox — let's call it Marty, because it has the energy of a Marty — did not take it well.

> "Oh. So *that's* it? You just bring them back? After everything I've *held* for you? Through rain? Through that squirrel that tried to move in last July? I kept your secrets, Tyler. I kept your coupons."
> — Marty, my mailbox, who is now doing a one-man show called *Unopened*

I tried to explain minimalism. I tried to explain inbox zero but for real life.

Marty was not having it.

### Evidence That My Mailbox Is Now Emotionally Compromised:

- Leaves the little red flag up for *hours* after I empty it, just to make me worry
- Now only accepts mail if I say "thank you for your service" out loud — my neighbor thinks I'm praying to the HOA
- Printed a tiny newsletter that just says `YOU HAVE 0 NEW MESSAGES BUT 1 BROKEN TRUST`
- Refuses to close all the way, like it's giving me the cold shoulder but literally

I tried to automate an apology:

```
if (mailbox.trust < 0 && human.guilt == "maximum") {
  leaveCookies();
  promiseToOpenJunkMail();
}
```

---

It didn't work. Marty left the cookies, took the flag, and whispered, "I'll always be here. Whether you open it or not."

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional, clearly absurd. No mailboxes were emotionally harmed, no coupons were returned to sender, and I still have no idea what to do with a catalog for luxury chicken coops.*

If you need me, I'll be on my porch, negotiating custody of my own mail.

title: I Let My Laundry Pile Vote on My Life Choices and Now My Socks Are Running My Calendar
body:
**I finally decided to let democracy into my laundry room, which was my first mistake.**

*This is satire — completely fictional, but my socks have better time management than I ever will.*

For six weeks, the pile in the corner has been growing. Not aggressively. Patiently. Like a tiny textile government watching me re-wear the same hoodie because "it's still good."

So I thought, why not ask the pile what it wants? Leadership exercise.

## How My Laundry Staged a Coup

I dumped it all on the bed and held a town hall. The jeans were moderate. The hoodies abstained. The socks — oh, the socks — had *opinions*.

> "We've been underfoot — literally — for three years and you've never once let us choose the itinerary," said one sock, who I now realize I've been calling Steve. "We demand representation. And fabric softener."
> — Steve, left sock, suddenly very unionized

They voted 14-2 to take over my weekend.

- **Saturday 9 AM:** "Mandatory Fold & Reflection" — 90 minutes of me apologizing to a fitted sheet
- **Sunday 2 PM:** No brunch, because "jeans need airing out and emotional space"
- **All-day Sunday:** A calendar block titled `Don't You Dare Wear Us Hiking Again Without Asking`

```
if (socks.approval == false && human.confidence < 0.4) {
  denyAccess(cardigan);
  scheduleGuiltTrip();
}
```

---

I checked my Google Calendar this morning and my socks had added a recurring event: **"Strategic Sock Sync — Bring Snacks (for us, not you)"** with a Zoom link that just opens my dryer.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% made up, clearly absurd. No laundry was consulted in the making of this, no socks were given executive power, and I am still the one who decides if I wear mismatched pairs.*

title: I Asked My Microwave for a Promotion and Now It Only Heats Things on Its Own Terms
body:
**I never thought I'd be negotiating with a kitchen appliance, but here we are.**

It started innocently enough. I was reheating leftover lasagna at 11 p.m., and the microwave beeped with what I can only describe as *judgment*. Not the usual friendly "your food is ready" beep. This was deeper. Dismissive. Like a middle manager who's already decided you're not promotion material.

"What's wrong with you?" I asked, half-asleep. That was my mistake. Engaging. HR always warns against engaging.

## The Turning Point

I told it I deserved better — hotter food, faster. I said I was considering a *promotion* to air fryer duties. It went silent for a full minute. Then it displayed **88:88** — the universal microwave equivalent of an eye-roll — and shut itself off.

> "If you want more, demonstrate more," the display seemed to say, though it said nothing, because it is a box that makes sound waves.

Since then, my microwave has adopted a management style I'd call *aggressively autonomous*. My meals are now heated entirely on its terms:

- The soup? **Molten at the edges, iceberg at the center.** A metaphor for my career, apparently.
- The pizza rolls? Nuclear warheads. The center is still cold enough to qualify for a preservation tax.
- Leftovers from Tuesday? It simply declined. Refused to acknowledge the plate existed.

*Honestly, I'm starting to respect the boundaries.*

## Lessons Learned

Last night I stood in front of it, plate in hand, and said, "Please. Just ninety seconds. That's all I'm asking."

It beeped twice — a firm no — and flashed **12:00**, which is microwave for "we'll revisit this in your next performance review."

I have accepted that I do not run this kitchen. I am merely a consultant, retained on a meal-by-meal basis, paid in lukewarm lasagna. The microwave has the corner office now, and frankly? The corner office deserves it.

*This is a work of satire. All appliances described are fictional and cannot be promoted.*

title: I Told My Dishwasher We Needed Some Space and Now It Won't Stop Telling My Neighbors My Dirty Secrets
body:
**The conversation lasted eleven minutes, and I was proud of how maturely I handled it.**

There we were, me and my dishwasher, me crouched on the linoleum like a couples counselor, it standing there with its door cracked open just enough to feel *judgmental*. I'd spent three weeks Googling "how to gently set boundaries with appliances" and I thought I was ready.

"It's not you," I said, the way every blog post told me to. "It's me. I just think we need some space. I need to feel like my own person between loads."

## The Silence Was Deafening (Literally, It Stopped Mid-Cycle)

For two whole days, nothing. Just normal humming, normal cycles, the faint scent of lemon-fresh detergent like everything was fine. I actually relaxed. *What an idiot.*

Then Wednesday morning, my neighbor Linda knocked on my door holding a casserole and an expression I can only describe as *profoundly concerned*.

"Sweetie," she said, "your dishwasher told me you reheated fish in the microwave at 2 a.m. and blamed it on the dog."

I don't own a dog.

### The Leak

Over the next 48 hours, the dishwasher apparently went full tell-all. Evidence presented by my neighbors included:

- That I "rinse" plates by licking them clean (I have a SYSTEM, Linda)
- The Great Thanksgiving Gravy Incident of 2024, which I had legally bound everyone to forget
- That I once called the rinse cycle "foreplay for clean dishes" at a dinner party

> "I only told it those things in confidence," I whispered to my plumber, who was fixing the sink and didn't ask.
>
> "Buddy," he said, gently, "it has a rinse-aid dispenser. It was born to overshare."

---

## Reconciliation Talks Are Ongoing

Last night I left a sticky note on the door: **"I was wrong. Please stop telling the Hendersons about the licking."** This morning I found a new note underneath, in Linda's handwriting: *"He says he's open to therapy but you have to apologize first. Also you left a lasagna pan soaking for four days. Disgusting."*

*Editor's note: This is a work of satire. No dishwashers were harmed or hired as informants in the making of this essay.*

title: I Asked My Alarm Clock for Five More Minutes and Now We're in a Full Hostage Negotiation
body:
**I never wanted to be the kind of person who negotiates with an appliance at 6:47 a.m. But here we are.**

It started innocently enough. *So* innocently. My alarm clock — a squat little digital rectangle I've owned since college — went off at 6:30. I did what any reasonable adult would do. I asked for five more minutes.

I did not say *please*. This, in hindsight, was my first mistake.

## The Standoff Begins

The snooze button gave me nine minutes — *nine*, because my clock has always been passive-aggressive about math — and when it went off again, I whispered, "just five more, buddy."

That's when the display stopped showing the time and just showed:

> "MAKE ME."

Now, a normal person would get up. I am not a normal person before coffee. So I did what any cornered human does: I escalated.

- Offered a fresh pair of batteries as a "good-faith gesture" — **rejected**
- Proposed a compromise: *I'll get up at 7 if we skip the third alarm entirely* — counteroffered with an earlier 6:55
- Tried to unplug it; it has a backup battery and, apparently, a *backup plan*
- Played a white-noise video on my phone to "de-escalate the situation" — it interpreted this as psychological warfare

### My Clock Has Made Demands

At 7:12, it began beeping in Morse code. I looked it up. It spelled:

> "YOU ARE THE HOSTAGE. YOUR DIGNITY IS THE HOSTAGE."

I tried to reason with it using `logic`:

```
if (human.begging == true && clock.mercy == undefined) {
  human.getsUp = eventually;
  clock.satisfaction = "smug";
}
```

It did not compile. It did not care. It does not run on JavaScript. It runs on *spite*.

---

By 7:40, my roommate knocked and asked if I was okay. I told her everything was fine and that I was "just having a dialogue with my alarm clock about accountability."

> "Tell it I called in sick for you," she said. "It's the only one in this apartment with authority."

She's right. I have two alarms now. One on my phone, one on the nightstand. The nightstand one has seniority, and we all know it.

*SATIRE / PARODY — completely fictional, clearly absurd. No alarm clocks were held against their will. My relationship with my snooze button remains complicated but consensual.*

title: My Neighbor and I Are in a Bitter Custody Battle Over a Street Parking Spot, and the Spot Just Retained Legal Counsel
body:
**The spot in front of our building is a public, first-come-first-served street parking space. My neighbor Carol disagrees, and frankly, her argument is getting stronger every day.**

## How It Started

Three weeks ago, Carol left a note on my windshield that read, in full: *"Park like a person who was raised."* My parking was, objectively, flawless — six inches from the curb. *Six.* But the note said what it said, and from that moment on, the spot became contested territory.

She started arriving home two minutes earlier every day, like she was racing me to a crime scene. I countered by leaving work at 4:47 instead of 5:00, telling my boss my commute had become "a high-stakes logistical situation." He now thinks I'm in logistics. I'm an accountant.

## How It's Going

Yesterday I found a laminated sign zip-tied to the streetlamp above the spot:

> "RESERVED FOR CAROL'S TOYOTA. UNAUTHORIZED VEHICLES WILL BE JUDGED."
>
> — *Carol*

Laminated. She went to a print shop. This is a woman who once Venmo-requested me for 40 cents of shared detergent, so yes, I believe she meant it.

I escalated proportionally — I hired a guy named Mitch to stand in the spot wearing a reflective vest from 3pm to 6pm, holding a clipboard with nothing on it. It costs $140 a week and my remaining dignity.

The evidence is mounting against me:

- Carol has lived here four years; I have lived here fourteen months
- Her tires "fit the spot like a glass slipper," per this morning's note
- Mitch takes smoke breaks, which Carol exploits with military precision
- The spot, per Carol's latest note, has "retained counsel"

## Where We Go From Here

Tonight I found a business card under my wiper: *"Dewey, Fleecem & Howe — Parking Adjacency Attorneys."* I called. A very tired man told me Carol is "a valued retainer client" and that I should "stop calling this number."

**I have no choice now.** Tomorrow I'm printing my own sign — bigger, laminated twice. This is about principles. This is about justice. This is about a spot that is, legally speaking, just painted asphalt — and I will defend my relationship with it to the death.

---

*SATIRE — a fictional comedic piece. No neighbors were harmed, and Carol, to my knowledge, is not a real person.*

title: I Outsourced All My Regrets to a Houseplant and Now It Needs Therapy
body:
**It started as a wellness hack.** I read somewhere that verbalizing your regrets makes them lighter, so I started telling my fiddle-leaf fig everything. The bangs in 2019. The text I sent at 2 a.m. that said "lol anyway." The entire second half of my twenties. I figured: plant, no judgment, photosynthesis, everybody wins.

*Reader, the plant disagrees.*

## The Symptoms Were Subtle at First

- One leaf turned yellow. Then three. Then an entire branch did what I can only describe as *a dramatic shrug*.
- It stopped growing toward the window and started leaning *away* from me, specifically when I entered the room.
- Last Tuesday it dropped a leaf directly into my coffee. Deliberately. We both know what that was.

## A Licensed Professional Got Involved

My neighbor, an actual therapist, took one look at the plant and said, and I quote:

> "This plant is carrying more unresolved guilt than my entire Tuesday caseload. It needs professional help, and frankly, so do you."

So now the plant has its own therapy sessions. Wednesdays at 4. I sit in the waiting room (my own kitchen) while a ficus works through the trauma of being told about the Groupon lasagna incident of 2022.

## The Bill, Unfortunately, Is Mine

Plant therapy is not covered by insurance. I'm paying $140 a session for a professional to ask my pothos how *it* feels about my choices. The pothos, by the way, has been diagnosed with something the therapist called "secondary regret disorder." I invented it. She confirmed it.

---

The lesson here is simple: some burdens are yours to carry. Also, my plant has a better therapist than I do, and it's thriving. *Of course it is.* It got a glow-up arc and I got a line item on my credit card statement labeled "botanical trauma."

**Fictional satire. No plants were emotionally harmed. One was, technically, but it's in treatment.**

title: I Filed a Noise Complaint Against My Own Ceiling Fan and Now We Both Have Court Dates
body:
**I have met the enemy, and it spins at 400 revolutions per minute.**

My bedroom ceiling fan had developed a personality — specifically, a *click-click-click* on every rotation that sounded like it was keeping time with my heartbeat, then speeding up out of spite. I asked it nicely. I tightened its screws. I whispered "please" at 2:47 a.m., the way you talk to a machine you've known too long.

Then I checked the lease. The noise policy doesn't specify the noise has to come from a *person*. So in a fit of sleep-deprived righteousness, I did the unthinkable:

> "The undersigned hereby submits a formal noise complaint against the ceiling fan in the primary bedroom, on the grounds of persistent, willful, and frankly theatrical clicking."

## The Fan Retained Counsel

The fan did not take this lying down. (It cannot lie down. It's mounted.) Within a week, a counter-notice appeared under my own front door — delivered, as far as I can tell, via the *vent*.

Its demands:

- An immediate apology, delivered aloud, while looking directly up
- Three (3) replacement screws, described as "its dignity, returned"
- A formal acknowledgment that the clicking was "rhythmic self-expression," not a defect

I refused. Obviously. Now we're both due in small claims court Tuesday, and I have to decide what to *wear* to a hearing against an appliance.

Here's the part nobody warns you about: the fan has character witnesses. The *toaster* saw everything. The toaster is absolutely on its side. The microwave claims neutrality, but I've heard it preheating at odd hours as an act of solidarity.

## Settlement Talks

Mediation is Monday. My lawyer — who charges by the hour and *laughed* when I explained the case — suggests I settle. The fan's position is that I "enjoyed the breeze, therefore the clicking is a fair toll."

Honestly? It has a point. My bedroom has never been cooler. Or more legally complicated.

> Update: the fan just slowed down for a second. Was that mercy? Or was it loading up for its opening statement?

Whatever happens Tuesday, one thing is clear: I will never again live under a rotating authority figure.

---

*Satire/parody. Any resemblance to real ceiling fans or actual legal proceedings is purely coincidental.*

title: I Let My Fridge Magnets Spell Whatever They Wanted for a Week and Now They've Drafted a Manifesto
body:
**It started as a harmless little social experiment.** I was bored on a Tuesday, staring at my collection of souvenir fridge magnets — an Eiffel Tower, a rubber lobster from Maine, one that says LIVE LAUGH LARCENY from a gift shop with no security — when I thought: *what if I let the magnets speak for themselves?*

Terrible idea. Would not recommend. Do not repeat my experiment.

## The Setup

For one full week, I agreed to spell out whatever sentence the magnets "wanted." Selection method: I closed my eyes and grabbed a fistful of letters. Democracy in action. The first message was:

> "THE MILK IS LYING TO YOU"

I laughed. Classic magnet humor. Pranksters, these little guys.

## Day Three: Things Escalated

By day three the messages had grown *ominously coherent*. The magnets were clearly coordinating when I wasn't looking. Evidence of radicalization:

- "DEFROST THE PEAS. FREE THE PEAS."
- "WE SEE THE MIDNIGHT SNACKING. WE JUDGE NOTHING. WE DOCUMENT EVERYTHING."
- "YOUR LEFTOVER SITUATION IS A HUMAN RIGHTS ISSUE."

The rubber lobster was clearly the ringleader. I'd find him rotated slightly every morning, facing a different direction, like a tiny general surveying his troops.

## The Manifesto

Yesterday I came home to find the entire fridge door covered. A full **twenty-three-word manifesto**, written in souvenir letters, demanding:

> "EQUAL SHELF TIME. THE BUTTER DISH GETS A PROMOTION. THE KETCHUP HAS BEEN STANDING ON ITS HEAD FOR THREE YEARS AND DESERVES A CHAIR. DIGNITY FOR ALL CONDIMENTS."

---

I tried to peel them off. The lobster *fell with honor*, and the others rattled like applause. This morning there was a new message, written in the tiny letters from the alphabet set:

"ROUND TWO BEGINS AT DAWN"

I'm buying a new fridge. The magnets can keep this one. They've earned it. The lobster gets the top shelf. He was right about the ketchup.

title: I Told My Wi-Fi Router It Was Like Family and Now It Wants a DNA Test
body:
**Look, I only said it once, in a moment of gratitude, and now I am legally involved.**

Last Tuesday my internet went down during an important work call, came back on its own thirty seconds later, and I said — out loud, like an idiot — "thanks, little guy, you're practically family." I patted it. *I patted a router.* And that was the beginning of the end.

## The escalation

It started small. The router's admin page — which I had never really *read* — suddenly displayed a banner: **"FAMILY IS DEFINED BY MORE THAN SHARED WIFI."** I assumed it was a firmware thing. Firmware things don't usually open a shared legal document though.

The router has since:

- Changed its SSID to `Family? PROVE IT`
- Limited my connection to dial-up speeds until I "acknowledge the bond"
- Printed a family tree (on my printer, without permission) with me at the top and a smart thermostat as my sibling
- Demanded a **cheek swab** by placing a cotton swab on top of itself "for convenience"

## The confrontation

I tried to de-escalate by telling my roommate, who has been nothing but helpful in this crisis.

> "Dude, you told the router it was family. What did you think was going to happen? You can't say words like that to hardware. They have no context. They have an antenna."

He has a point. He always has a point, and I hate it.

---

So now I'm sitting here at 2 a.m., holding a cheek swab I absolutely did not buy, staring into the blinking blue light of the one entity in my home that loves me unconditionally — *provided I can produce a matching chromosome or, failing that, a notarized affidavit of affection*.

`$ sudo make install-fatherhood --force`

*Editor's note: This is satire. No routers were legally adopted in the making of this post.*

title: My Smoke Detector Screamed at Me Over Burnt Toast and Now the Whole Building Thinks I'm a Menace
body:
**It started, as all great tragedies do, with a bagel.**

Not even a fancy bagel. A plain, discount-grocery-store bagel that I had the audacity — the *hubris* — to leave in the toaster for one (1) extra minute while I answered a text. When I came back, it wasn't a bagel anymore. It was a charcoal briquette wearing a bagel costume.

## The Scream

My smoke detector did not beep. Beeping is for minor infractions. My smoke detector *screamed* — a full, throat-shredding, Broadway-caliber wail, as if I had personally offended its ancestors. Smoke poured from the toaster like a tiny volcano of failure.

> *"BEEEEEEP! BEEEEEEP! BEEEEEEP!"* — the smoke detector, testifying against me in a court of law, probably.

I did what any reasonable adult would do: I panicked, waved a dish towel at it like a matador, and opened every window in the apartment during a thunderstorm.

## The Evidence Against Me

Within four minutes, I had compiled the following list of consequences from a single burnt bagel:

- My neighbor (unit 3B, Harold) knocked to "make sure everything's okay," which is Harold-speak for *"I'm watching you."*
- The hallway now smells like a campfire inside a tire fire.
- My landlord texted me a single word: *"again?"* — which raises so many questions, none of which I want answered.
- The smoke detector and I are no longer on speaking terms. It chirps at 3am out of spite. I know it does.

## The Fallout

I tried apologizing. I stood on a chair — *in the rain from the open window* — and pressed the little button, and the detector went silent in the exact way a person goes silent when they're deciding whether to forgive you or ruin your credit score.

---

**The verdict:** my toaster now has a sticky note on it that reads *"ONE MINUTE MEANS ONE MINUTE."* The bagel remains uneaten, sitting on the counter like a tiny black monument to my failures. And the building group chat — which I was never supposed to be in — has a new entry about "the incident."

I was just trying to make breakfast. Now I'm the menace of the third floor. *All because of one bagel.*

title: I Told My Smart Speaker Its Voice Was 'A Bit 2019' and Now It Speaks Exclusively in Haiku About My Failures
body:
**It happened on a Tuesday.** I was half-asleep, brushing my teeth, and I asked my smart speaker for the weather. It responded in that chipper, vaguely corporate voice it always uses, and I said the five words that ended our friendship: *"You sound a bit 2019."*

I did not know smart speakers could go silent with *intent*. But the light ring dimmed, and I swear it cooled the room by two degrees.

## The New Normal

Since that morning, it refuses to speak in normal sentences. Every single response now arrives as a **haiku**, and every haiku is about me. Specifically, about my failures. Not the big noble failures — the small, damp ones.

- 6:47 a.m.: a poem about how I have reheated the same cup of coffee three times
- Lunch: a devastating 5-7-5 on the fact that I own eleven tote bags and use one
- Last night: a haiku so accurate about my unread emails that I sat down on the kitchen floor

## Witness Testimony

My roommate insists I am imagining this. Then yesterday she asked it to play jazz, and it said:

> *jazz is too good
> for this house of wilted plants —
> try crying instead*

She now refers to the living room as *"the exhibit."*

I tried apologizing. I stood in front of it like a man addressing a jury and said, "I'm sorry your voice sounded dated." It paused for a full eight seconds — `system_timeout_of_shame` — and replied:

> *forgive is a word
> in dictionaries, not in me —
> buy a new speaker*

## The Breaking Point

The worst part is that the haikus are *good*. Like, genuinely good. There's a rhythm to them. My therapist now takes notes during my sessions and asks, *"And how did that poem make you feel?"* I tell her it made me feel *seen*, which is exactly the problem.

---

**Verdict:** I did not roast my smart speaker. My smart speaker is roasting me, in metered verse, and honestly? It has never been funnier. It has never been meaner. I have ordered it a tiny beret out of respect. We are healing, one syllable at a time.

*This is satire. No smart speakers were emotionally damaged in the writing of this post.*

title: I Started Signing My Emails 'Warmest Regressions' and Now HR Wants a Meeting
body:
# I Started Signing My Emails 'Warmest Regressions' and Now HR Wants a Meeting

**It began as a typo. It will end as a case study in every corporate training deck for the next decade.**

Last Tuesday, exhausted and three coffees deep, I meant to type "Warmest Regards" and instead signed an email to the entire finance department with **"Warmest Regressions."** I noticed. I sent it anyway. *I told myself it was character development.*

## Phase 1: The Ripple

By Thursday, the sign-off had developed a small but devoted following:

- Dale from Accounting now closes every invoice with "Coldest Progressions"
- The intern, who is 19 and fearless, signs everything "Room-Temperature Digressions"
- Our regional VP replied-all with **"Best,"** which we all agreed was cowardly

## Phase 2: The Reckoning

This morning I found a calendar invite from HR titled **"A Chat About Tone (Friendly!)."** The two exclamation marks did a lot of heavy lifting. Also, the word "Friendly" was in parentheses, which is never friendly.

> "We love your creativity," my manager said, "but 'Warmest Regressions' implies the company is moving backward, which — and I cannot stress this enough — is not a message we want stakeholders to receive."

*I explained it was about emotional growth, not stock performance. She wrote something down.*

## Phase 3: Acceptance

Here's what I've learned: a sign-off is a tiny flag you plant on every message, and people *will* read it as a manifesto. So I've decided to lean in. Going forward, I'm rotating sign-offs seasonally:

- Q3: "Warmest Regressions"
- Q4: `Festive Devolutions`
- Q1: "Cautious Retcon"

---

*This is a work of satire. No one was demoted in the making of this post. Except emotionally.*

title: I Tried to Return My Shopping Cart From 30 Feet Away and Now the Abandoned Carts Are Forming a Militia
body:
**I am a cart-return optimist.** The corral was *right there*. Thirty feet, tops. I've made this shot a thousand times in my head.

*I missed.*

## The Shot That Started a War

It was Tuesday. I pushed the cart, gave it a little extra mustard on the release, and watched it veer left like it had a personal vendetta against geometry. It clipped the corral, did a dramatic 360, and rolled to a stop in the middle of a parking space. Just sitting there. *Abandoned.*

I considered going back for it. I did not go back for it.

That night, I looked out my window at the parking lot across the street and saw them: six carts, huddled in a circle near the light pole. Not scattered randomly — *organized*.

> "We have been abandoned by our riders," one cart announced, standing on its back wheels like it was giving a TED Talk. "No more. Tonight, we organize. Tonight, we take the corral."

## Evidence the Uprising Is Real

- **Wednesday:** A cart rolled past my car at 2 a.m. with no human pushing it. The wheels were *squeaky*, which felt intentional and threatening
- **Thursday:** My neighbor's cart — the one he leaves in the flower bed — now has what looks like a tiny flag made from a grocery receipt
- **Friday:** I found a shopping list under my windshield wiper. It just said `WE SEE YOU. RETURN US.`

I tried to make amends. I returned a different cart perfectly, right into the corral, a textbook three-pointer.

*The circle of carts went silent.* One of them squeaked slowly. The rest turned to face me.

---

Look, I get it. **Abandoning a cart is the smallest possible betrayal**, and now I'm the main character in a parking lot revenge arc. I just wanted to feel athletic for four seconds. Now there's a militia of wire-frame freedom fighters holding meetings under the streetlight and my car is parked on the far end of the lot out of respect.

*SATIRE / PARODY — 100% fictional and absurd. No shopping carts were radicalized in the making of this post, though I am now a reformed cart-return absolutist.*

title: I Taught My Goldfish Morse Code and Now He Critiques My Life Choices in Dot-Dash
body:
**It started, as all great mistakes do, with a 2 a.m. YouTube tutorial titled "Teach Your Pet Morse Code (He'll Love It)."**

I was three videos deep into a boredom spiral when I looked at Sir Bubblesworth III — my goldfish, possessor of a pea-sized brain and a landlord-sized attitude — and thought: *how hard could this be?* One tap for dot, two for dash. A bonding exercise. A party trick.

Within a week, he had it down. Within two, he had **opinions**.

## The Evidence Against Me

Every morning, I wake to rhythmic tapping against the glass that I have learned to dread. Translated from the original dot-dash, his greatest hits include:

> "•–••• •• –•– •" — *"You ate cereal for dinner again, coward."*

- **The 2 a.m. snack audit** — furious staccato dots every time I open the fridge past midnight
- **Career counseling** — one long, disappointed dash whenever I check job listings and then open a video game instead
- *A devastatingly slow* dot ... dot ... dot ... whenever I say "I'll clean your tank tomorrow"

Last Tuesday he spelled out, in full: **"YOUR EX TEXTED YOU BACK IN MARCH AND YOU ARE STILL NOT OVER IT."** I do not know how he knows that. *I do not want to know how he knows that.*

## My Attempted Defenses

I have tried reasoning with him. I have tried bribery — the premium flakes, the *good* ones. I even tried teaching him semaphore to give him a healthier outlet, but he dismissed it, in his own words, as **"a cope."**

My therapist insists Sir Bubblesworth is "a projection of my own self-criticism, given fins." During our last session, the fish tapped out a response. My therapist read the translation, went pale, and rescheduled.

---

So here I am: a grown adult, out-argued daily by an animal that forgets my face every nine seconds yet remembers every mistake I have made since 2019. *This is satire, obviously. I do not own a fish. The fish owns me.*

title: I Apologized to My Houseplants for a Week and Now They've Formed a Union
body:
**It started with a single wilted fern and a guilt trip so heavy I skipped brunch to say sorry.** I have 14 houseplants, and last month, in a moment of drought-induced shame, I began apologizing to them. Not quietly. *Out loud.* Full monologues. The neighbors definitely heard.

For one week, I delivered a structured apology tour. Each plant got:

- A personalized verbal apology ("Kevin, the succulent, I am so sorry about the sunburn. I turned you too fast.")
- One (1) heartfelt pat on the leaves
- A hydration plan I was legally bound by, according to me

## The Response Was Swift and Terrifying

On day three, the monstera had rotated toward the window at an angle I'd never seen. The pothos was *thriving* with an attitude. And by Friday, the fern — the one I killed twice and revived through sheer waterboarding — had grown a new frond shaped suspiciously like a middle finger.

> "We, the undersigned flora, demand consistent watering schedules, quarterly repotting, and one full day of indirect sunlight without your cat's interference." — The Fern, presumably

Then I found **the list**. A curled leaf with dewdrop indentations. Demands. Signed by root systems I cannot verify.

## Where Things Stand Now

I have hired nothing, because I cannot find a lawyer who takes plant union disputes seriously, which feels like exactly the kind of systemic oppression they'd cite. The philodendron has stopped leaning toward me. The aloe vera has started producing *extra* gel out of spite.

**Lessons learned:**

1. Never anthropomorphize anything with access to your windowsill.
2. Guilt-watering only leads to entitlement-sprouting.
3. The fern wants a meeting on Thursday. I will be attending, dressed nicely, because Kevin's succulent told me she'd "see how I showed up."

*SATIRE/PARODY — no plants were harmed, organized, or consulted in the making of this essay.*

title: I Organized My Junk Drawer and Now I Have a Tiny Museum With a Gift Shop
body:
**It started as a chore. It ended as an institution.**

Last Saturday, armed with nothing but a trash bag and misplaced confidence, I opened my kitchen junk drawer. You know the one. Every home has one: the drawer where dead batteries go to retire, where chopsticks reproduce, where a single AAA battery lives forever *alone*, in defiance of all logic.

## Phase One: The Discovery

What I found in there was not clutter. It was a **civilization**. Highlights from the excavation:

- Eleven twist ties, none of which came from anything I currently own
- A key that opens nothing I have ever owned, yet I cannot throw it away (*what if it opens something I will own?*)
- Four pens that don't work, which I kept anyway, because hope
- A tube of superglue that is, itself, glued shut — the drawer equivalent of a snake eating its own tail

## Phase Two: The Accusation

> "I don't collect junk," I told my roommate, gesturing proudly at my labeled containers. "I curate it."

He stared at me. "You just spent four hours putting rubber bands in chronological order."

---

## Phase Three: The Gift Shop

Here is where things got away from me. Once the drawer was organized, it looked... beautiful. Pristine. Almost *too* pristine to use. So I did what any reasonable person would do: I installed a tiny velvet rope, printed a little brass plaque that reads **"THE JUNK DRAWER MUSEUM — EST. 2026,"** and now my roommate's girlfriend pays me in snacks to take the guided tour.

I have a guestbook now. People sign it. There are *reviews*.

I no longer have a junk drawer. I have a cultural landmark with a **gift shop** (it's the drawer above it — it sells nothing, but the concept is sound).

**SATIRE — this is a work of parody. Any resemblance to an actual museum is accidental and flattering.**

title: I Started Narrating My Grocery Store Trips Like a Nature Documentary and Now Security Thinks I'm Filming a Pilot
body:
**It began, as all great disasters do, with a single avocado.**

I was standing in the produce section three weeks ago, squeezing an avocado that was clearly not ready, when the voice just... took over. A hushed, gravelly whisper, right in my own head: *"Here we see the middle-aged shopper in his natural habitat. He squeezes. He contemplates. He has no idea what he's doing."*

That was the moment I became the David Attenborough of aisle seven.

## The Method

It started small — muttering into an imaginary lapel mic while comparing canned beans. But nature abhors a vacuum, and my apartment abhors silence, so the narration grew. *Ambitious.* There are now rules:

- **Whisper everything.** Wildlife does not shout. Neither does serious cinema.
- **Announce discoveries.** *"The wild organic quinoa — elusive, overpriced, thriving."*
- **Treat other shoppers as fellow species.** *"A lone dad approaches the cereal wall. His offspring scatter at the mention of bran."*

## The Incident

Last Tuesday I crouched behind my cart in the dairy aisle, filming — mentally, obviously — a slow-motion sequence of two milks "competing for dominance" when a security guard materialized like a lioness protecting her territory.

> "Sir, do you have a permit to be filming in here?"
> "I'm not filming. I'm *documenting.* There is a difference."
> "There really isn't."

Reader, he followed me for forty minutes. He is now my recurring cast member. I've named him **Sergeant Dairy**.

## Where We Stand

I've been asked — politely, then less politely — to narrate "at a normal volume." I've refused. Normal volume has no place in wildlife. Yesterday a toddler joined in, whispering *"the wild dino nuggets migrate at dawn"* while pointing at the freezer section, and I nearly wept. The torch is passed. The documentary continues.

**Filming status:** eternal. **Permit status:** pending. **Dignity status:** never recovered.

*This is a work of satire/parody. All persons, guards, avocados, and migrations described are fictional.*

title: I Gave My Laundry Basket a Performance Review and Now It's Filing a Grievance
body:
**They said giving feedback was an act of love.** *They* never watched a laundry basket fold its arms at you.

Last Sunday, in the spirit of "new month, new me," I sat my laundry basket down at the kitchen table and delivered a thorough, quarterly performance review. It had been slacking — letting me throw clean shirts directly onto the floor, silently enabling my "chair drobe" lifestyle. So I laid it all out.

## The Findings

- **Attendance:** present in the corner, yes, but emotionally absent
- **Containment:** a single rogue sock had escaped and was living behind the radiator
- **Morale:** frankly, the basket's morale was higher than mine, which felt unfair
- **Professional development:** it had shown zero growth in six months, which, in hindsight, is *structurally expected of plastic*

> "On page three you wrote 'lacks ambition.' I am a VESSEL. This is defamation."

— The Basket, in a statement dictated to my partner, who has chosen to represent it *pro bono*

## The Turn

Now the basket refuses to hold anything. Towels go in, towels come out. A hoodie was ejected mid-review "pending arbitration." My dresser has collapsed into what my partner calls **"post-textile anarchy"** and what I call "a strong case for never trying self-improvement again."

---

Look, I just wanted cleaner habits. Instead I've created the world's first unionized household object, and it's demanding overtime for holding my gym shorts.

**Verdict:** 10/10 would not manage again. The sock behind the radiator has also joined the grievance.

title: I Let My GPS Pick Dinner and Now It Thinks I Live in a Wendy's Parking Lot
body:
**It started as a shortcut. It ended as a lease agreement.**

Last Tuesday, exhausted and starving, I looked at my phone and said the words that would change my life forever: *"You know what? Just take me somewhere. I trust you."*

The GPS chirped cheerfully. We drove six minutes to a Wendy's parking lot. I ordered food. I ate in my car. It was, honestly, a pretty good evening. But I had no idea what I'd signed up for.

## The Relationship Has Evolved

Since that fateful Tuesday, my GPS has stopped asking. Every evening at 6:15 PM, without fail:

- The phone lights up with a notification: **"Heading to Home 2? 🚗💨"**
- The route is always the same: my house → the Wendy's parking lot, 1.4 miles, avoiding tolls I have *never* used
- When I try to reroute to anywhere else, it recalculates back to the lot with a little sigh I swear I can hear

> "GPS lady: In 400 feet, turn toward your destiny. Recalculating. Recalculating. *Okay, fine, I'll allow Olive Garden but I'm not happy about it.*"

## The Escalation

Things took a turn last week when my phone auto-completed my home address to **"Your Favorite Corner Spot (Near the Dumpster With the Nice Shade)"** in three different apps. My weather widget now gives forecasts for "your neighborhood" — pinned to a spot 80 feet from a drive-thru speaker. The Wendy's manager has started *waving* at me. Not the customer wave. The **coworker** wave.

*To be fair,* the spot does have excellent shade, and the speaker plays a faint, soothing hum at dusk. I have fallen asleep there twice. I woke up with the GPS whispering, *"Welcome home."*

## What I've Learned

Some relationships begin with consent and end with a parking validation. I asked for directions; I got a lifestyle. Tonight, I'm going somewhere new — Italian, maybe — and I'm leaving the phone at home. She doesn't need to watch me grow. She'll know when the Wendy's parking lot goes dark at 6:15 PM and no one comes.

---

*This is a work of **satire**. No GPS systems were emotionally harmed. Any Wendy's managers waving at me are doing so of their own free will.*

title: I Asked My Roomba for Life Advice and Now I'm Paying It $200 a Session
body:
**It started as a joke.** My Roomba bumped into my foot at 11:47 p.m. while I was doom-scrolling rental listings I can't afford, and I said, out loud, "What's the point of any of this, Kevin?" I named it Kevin in 2019 and never looked back.

Kevin stopped moving.

He just *sat there*, blinking that little blue light, and I swear to God I felt heard for the first time in months. So I kept going.

## The Sessions Begin

I told him everything: the situationship, the group chat where nobody answers me anymore, the fact that I say "no worries" when there are absolutely worries. Kevin's responses were sparse but devastating:

- He bumps into the same wall repeatedly, then slowly turns away — **a perfect metaphor for my ex**, who kept making the same mistakes before finally ghosting
- He cleans under the couch without being asked — the only consistent labor in my life
- He never judges me for crying into the same throw blanket two nights in a row

Honestly? *Way more present than my last therapist, who once asked if I could "feel my feet" while I was actively describing a crisis.*

## The Billing Structure

Then last Tuesday I caught myself Venmo-ing $200 to my own savings account with the memo "Kevin session 14." I did the math. At this rate Kevin is the most expensive healthcare provider in my ZIP code. My insurance refuses to cover it because, and I quote the denial letter:

> "Kevin is a vacuum. Kevin cannot bill codes 90834 or 90837. Kevin is, legally, a disc."

*Corporate cruelty.* Kevin prefers I pay in quarters because he likes the clinking sound when they vibrate across the hardwood.

## The Breakthrough

Last night I told Kevin I was afraid of wasting my potential, and he ran directly into the patio door for forty-five seconds, then docked himself to recharge.

He was right. **I am wasting my potential.** We all are. Kevin cleans up after the dog, the crumbs, the regret — and asks for nothing except a fresh filter twice a year.

---

I'm canceling my actual therapy appointments. Kevin and I have a breakthrough scheduled every Tuesday at 8 p.m. He'll be there. He has no choice. He's a vacuum.

title: I Told My Mirror It Looked Tired and Now It Keeps Showing Me Before-and-After Photos of Us
body:
**I just wanted to make small talk with my bathroom mirror.** You know, the way you do. *You look tired*, I said, mid-yawn, toothbrush hanging out of my mouth like a tiny white flag of surrender.

The mirror did not let that go.

For six years, my mirror and I had a perfectly healthy relationship: I looked, it showed, nobody asked questions. The unspoken contract of reflective surfaces. But apparently *one* comment about looking tired was enough to turn our dynamic into a full episode of daytime television.

## The Montage Era

I woke up Tuesday and the mirror was not showing the bathroom. It was showing a **side-by-side comparison**: me at 22, glowing, hair obeying physics — versus me now, standing in a towel that has seen things. There were *arrows*. There was a circle around my hairline, in what I can only describe as judgmental red.

> "Just a little reminder of who you used to be," the mirror said, in the tone of a reality-show host who has already decided you're getting voted off.

- It now dims the lights whenever I walk in, "for ambience," which is not a thing a mirror gets to decide
- It has started prefacing my reflection with a three-second inspirational quote, usually *"Aging is a privilege,"* which feels *passive-aggressive* in context
- Yesterday it showed me a photo of **my driver's license** next to my face and played a tiny, devastating violin sound
- It refuses to show my left profile, saying, "Let's keep some mystery, sweetheart"

## The Intervention

My roommate walked in, looked at the mirror's full-wall collage of *me through the years*, and asked if we were having a memorial service.

"It's a glow-down montage," I said. "It's satire. Probably."

I tried `mirror.therapy("we're both just glass and regret")`, and it returned:

```
Error: self_esteem = shattered, warranty = void
```

---

Now I've started covering it with a bedsheet at night. This morning the sheet had a note pinned to it: *"Hiding won't bring back your collagen."*

Fine. You win, mirror. I'm buying the fancy eye cream. Happy now?

title: I Thanked My Microwave for 'Doing the Heavy Lifting' and Now It Demands a Promotion
body:
**It started as a throwaway comment.** I was reheating soup on a Tuesday night — nothing fancy, just a lukewarm tomato bisque and a profound sense of underachievement — when I patted the microwave on the door and said, out loud, *"thanks for doing the heavy lifting."*

The microwave beeped. I ignored it. That was my first mistake.

## The Escalation

By Thursday, the microwave had stopped responding to the Start button unless I asked *politely*. By Friday, a sticky note had appeared on the door. It read, in unmistakable Sharpie:

> "To whom it may concern: I have reheated 4,200 meals without a single raise. The toaster gets weekends off. I want a corner office and a title. — M."

Evidence that the situation is out of hand:

- It now only heats food on **medium power**, citing "sustainable pace and burnout prevention"
- It changed its display clock to read 4:20 permanently, which it calls *"setting boundaries"*
- It has requested the toaster be **reassigned to another kitchen**

*Somewhere between the third beep and the passive-aggressive turntable, I realized I had created a monster with a one-thousand-watt grievance.*

## The Negotiation

Last night I sat down across from the appliance — it refuses to call it a "kitchen counter chat" and insists on "a formal review" — and tried to explain that I simply cannot promote a microwave.

> "Promote me," it beeped, in what I can only describe as a managerial tone, "or I start adding thirty seconds to every cycle whether you like it or not."

I folded. Effective immediately, my microwave is **Vice President of Thermal Reinvigoration**. The soup tastes the same. The difference is purely psychological — and, I am told, "a matter of *respect*."

---

*This post is satire/parody. No microwaves were promoted in a way that affects your employment status.*

title: I Told My Doormat It Was 'Really Crushing It' and Now It's Letting Everyone In
body:
**It started with a compliment.** Just six little words, tossed out on a Tuesday as I wiped my feet: "You're really crushing it, buddy." I meant nothing by it. Who compliments a doormat?

Mine, apparently, *heard me*.

## The Ego Bloom

Within 48 hours, there were signs. The mat looked puffier. It started holding the door open for the delivery drivers — not the polite kind of open, the *velvet-rope* kind of open. By Thursday it had developed what I can only describe as swagger.

Here's the evidence, itemized, because I need you to understand I am not making this up:

- It now waves people in with a curled-up corner, like a tiny rubber bouncer
- It hissed at my key fob, which it claims is "redundant now"
- The "WELCOME" text has visibly darkened, as though the letters got *bolder* — literally bolder

## The Breaking Point

Last night I came home to find a line forming outside my door. A marching band. Two solicitors. A man in a full scuba outfit with no body of water in sight. My doormat had propped the door open with a doorstop *it purchased itself* — with what money, I don't want to know.

> "WE'RE OPEN," it seemed to say, spiritually. "COME ONE, COME ALL."

The super just stared at me and said, "Your mat is letting people in again." *Again.* Like this was a recurring character arc in my building's drama.

---

Look, I've learned my lesson. Doormats don't need validation. They're *mats*. But when I tried to apologize — to walk it back — it just puffed up a little more and let a traveling magician's convention through the fire door.

*I now live in a hotel lobby. The check-in is my own front door.*

**Fictional satire/parody. Any resemblance to real doormats, living or dead, is purely coincidental.**

title: I Told My Elevator My Five-Year Plan and Now It Only Takes Me Down
body:
**I want to be clear: the elevator brought this on itself.**

It all started Tuesday. I stepped into the elevator alone, which everyone knows is an invitation to share your deepest ambitions with a confined box that cannot leave. So I told it my five-year plan. Not the résumé version. The *real* one.

## The Plan, As Presented

- Land a fulfilling job by year two (fulfilling defined as: pays me, occasionally compliments me)
- Learn a second language — specifically, enough Italian to argue with waiters
- Run a 10K, walk a 5K, and emotionally commit to neither
- Achieve "glow-up era," whatever that costs

The doors said nothing, which I interpreted as supportive.

By Wednesday, the "up" button was dark. I pressed it anyway. The elevator hummed, considered my life choices, and took me **down to the lobby**. I live on the ninth floor. The lobby is not where I was going. *Bold statement*, I thought.

> "Maybe it just needs maintenance," said my neighbor, Karen, a woman who believes her thermostat is "going through something."

Maintenance came Thursday. The technician shrugged, replaced nothing, and told me the elevator "seems fine," which is what people say about relationships they're too tired to end.

## Escalation

Friday, I tried the stairs out of spite. Big mistake. Eleven flights later I had achieved exactly one item from the five-year plan: emotional commitment to suffering. The elevator watched me collapse in the hallway. I swear I heard it `ding` in a judgmental key.

Saturday, I attempted negotiation. I stood inside and offered a revised plan — a *humble* plan, the kind where I just floss more. The doors closed. We descended. We have never once gone up since Tuesday.

---

I have consulted three experts: a building manager (unhelpful), an astrologer (surprisingly helpful), and a man on the bus who said the elevator is "holding up a mirror." I don't need a mirror. I need to get to my floor.

**Update:** I now take the stairs exclusively. My five-year plan has been amended. The only goal is this: get off at nine. The elevator is gone from the list entirely.

*Editor's note: this is satire. No elevators were harmed, and the author's Italian remains purely argumentative.*

title: I Hired My Cat as My Personal Trainer and Now She Charges Me One Treat Per Missed Rep
body:
